title: United Arab Emirates | CBUAE AML/CFT/CPF Compliance
tagline: The UAE's 2025 AML/CFT/CPF law in practice: offences, CDD, goAML reporting, sanctions freezing and your bank's programme.
sectors: Onshore conventional banks licensed by the CBUAE
description:
A country-specific quest for staff of **onshore conventional banks supervised by the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE)**. It is built on **Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025** on anti-money laundering and combating the financing of terrorism and proliferation financing, its executive regulations in **Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025**, **Cabinet Resolution No. 74 of 2020** on targeted financial sanctions, guidance from the **Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation (EOCN)**, reporting to the **UAE Financial Intelligence Unit** through goAML, and the CBUAE's role as supervisor.

The executive regulations require banks to run periodic AML/CFT/CPF capacity-building programmes and make the compliance officer responsible for ongoing, documented employee training, so this quest is aimed at everyone from branch tellers to board members. You will learn the three offences, the risk-based approach, CDD, beneficial ownership and PEP rules, how to escalate and report suspicion without tipping off, what to keep and for how long, how to screen, freeze and report under UAE sanctions rules, how to spot proliferation financing in trade, and what the CBUAE expects of your institution's programme.

The DIFC and ADGM financial free zones have their own regulators and rulebooks and are mentioned only as separate regimes.

This quest builds knowledge of the UAE framework; it does not replace your institution's own AML/CFT/CPF policies and procedures, which you must always follow.
audience: All employees of CBUAE-licensed onshore conventional banks who need AML/CFT/CPF induction or refresher training
Branch, call-centre and relationship staff who onboard customers and handle cash, transfers and customer questions
Onboarding, KYC, screening and transaction monitoring teams who apply CDD, EDD and sanctions controls
Trade finance, correspondent banking and payments staff exposed to proliferation financing and sanctions evasion
Compliance officers, internal auditors, senior managers and board members accountable for the AML/CFT/CPF programme
outcomes: Explain the UAE AML/CFT/CPF framework, its three offences and the roles of the CBUAE, the UAE FIU, the EOCN and the National Committee
Apply the risk-based approach and the 2025 executive regulations to CDD, EDD, simplified measures, beneficial ownership and PEPs
Escalate suspicion internally, support a goAML suspicious transaction report, avoid tipping off and keep records for the required period
Screen against the UAE Local Terrorist List and the UN Consolidated List, freeze without delay and file the right goAML report
Recognise proliferation financing and sanctions evasion red flags in trade and payments
Describe the compliance officer's duties, role-based training, senior management accountability, independent audit and supervisory penalties

quest.name: Guardians of the Gate
quest.premise: You have just joined the Financial Crime Compliance team of Lumara Bank, a fictional onshore conventional bank licensed by the CBUAE, with its head office in Abu Dhabi and branches in Dubai, Sharjah and Al Ain. The UAE's 2025 AML/CFT/CPF law and its new executive regulations are in force, and the CBUAE has scheduled an AML inspection. With compliance officer Maryam Al Suwaidi, branch manager Rashid Al Ketbi, analyst Priya Raman and trade finance manager Joseph Mwangi, clear five stages, then face the final boss: briefing chief executive Khalid Al Hosani and the board.

badge.name: UAE AML Gatekeeper

sessions.title: The UAE Framework: Laws, Offences and Who Supervises

cards.title: Day one at Lumara Bank
cards.setting: Financial Crime Compliance floor, Lumara Bank head office, Abu Dhabi. 8:45 am.

lines.text: Your access card works on the second try. On your desk: a laptop, a lanyard and a sticky note that says 'See Maryam. Urgent.'
Welcome to Lumara. I'm Maryam, the bank's compliance officer. You've arrived at an interesting time.
The UAE replaced its AML law in 2025, new executive regulations followed, and the CBUAE has just scheduled an AML inspection of us.
(on a video call from Deira) Rashid here. My tellers keep asking me: is money laundering a police matter or our problem?
And my monitoring team wants to know which old article numbers in our procedures still mean anything.
Good questions. Before anyone can answer them, we all need the same map: which laws apply, what the offences are and who does what.
Stage one is the Rulebook Tower. Climb it with me and you'll be able to answer Rashid's tellers by lunchtime.

cards.title: The UAE framework in five scenes

scenes.heading: The law at the top
scenes.narration: Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 is the UAE's anti-money laundering law. It creates the offences, sets penalties and lists the core duties of banks.

scenes.heading: The rules underneath
scenes.narration: Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 is its executive regulation. It turns the law's duties into detail: risk assessment, due diligence, reporting, training and record keeping.

scenes.heading: Your supervisor
scenes.narration: For onshore banks, the Central Bank of the UAE is the supervisory authority. It inspects banks, issues guidance in its Rulebook and can impose administrative penalties.

scenes.heading: Where reports go
scenes.narration: Suspicious transaction reports go only to the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit, an independent unit inside the Central Bank, through its electronic system, goAML.

scenes.heading: Sanctions in a separate lane
scenes.narration: The Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation runs targeted financial sanctions under Cabinet Resolution 74 of 2020. The DIFC and ADGM free zones have their own regulators and rulebooks.

cards.title: Layers of the UAE framework
cards.caption: Each layer must fit the one above it. Your bank's policies turn all of them into daily procedures.

items.label: Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025
items.detail: The federal AML/CFT/CPF law: offences, penalties and core duties of financial institutions.

items.label: Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025
items.detail: Executive regulations: risk assessment, CDD, PEPs, STRs, compliance officer, training, records.

items.label: Cabinet Resolution 74 of 2020
items.detail: Targeted financial sanctions: UAE Local Terrorist List and UN list implementation.

items.label: CBUAE and EOCN guidance
items.detail: Supervisory guidance that explains how banks should meet the legal duties.

items.label: Lumara's own policies
items.detail: Approved by senior management and binding on every employee.

cards.title: Who does what in the UAE?
cards.prompt: Match each authority to its role in the AML/CFT/CPF system.

pairs.right: Supervises onshore banks, inspects them and can impose administrative penalties
Receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports filed through goAML
Oversees targeted financial sanctions and sends list updates to registered entities
Sets national AML/CFT/CPF strategy and assesses national risk; chaired by the CBUAE Governor
Separate regulators for the DIFC and ADGM financial free zones

cards.question: A Lumara analyst concludes a payment is suspicious. Under the 2025 law, where must the report go?
options: Only to the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit, through its electronic system
To the CBUAE banking supervision department by email
To the police station nearest the branch
To the EOCN, because it handles all financial crime
cards.explanation: The decree-law makes the FIU, an independent unit established within the Central Bank, the exclusive recipient of suspicious transaction reports, filed through its electronic system (goAML). Supervision is a separate CBUAE function, and the EOCN deals with sanctions.

cards.title: Three offences, one law
cards.body:
Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 sets out three crimes:

- **Money laundering (Article 2):** dealing with proceeds of a predicate offence while knowing, or having sufficient indications to believe, they are criminal: converting or transferring them to hide their origin, concealing their true nature or ownership, acquiring or using them, or helping the offender escape punishment. It is an **independent crime**, and no conviction for the predicate offence is needed.
- **Terrorist financing (Article 3(1)):** providing or collecting funds by any means, including virtual assets, knowing they will be used for terrorist acts, terrorists or terrorist travel. Clean money counts too.
- **Proliferation financing (Article 3(3)):** funding weapons of mass destruction, their delivery means or related dual-use goods. It is now a standalone offence.

Knowledge can be **inferred from the facts**, and a bank itself can be criminally liable (Article 4).

cards.title: ML, TF or PF?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation into the offence it most likely points to.

items.text: Bribe money is moved through three company accounts to hide where it came from
A salaried employee sends small sums to pay for a friend's travel to join an armed group
A trading firm pays for machine parts that are listed dual-use goods bound for a weapons programme
Fraud proceeds are used to buy a villa in a relative's name
A charity collection is diverted to a designated terrorist organisation
A front company settles freight for sanctioned missile components
Cash from smuggling is mixed into a restaurant's daily takings

cards.title: Rashid's free-zone question
cards.setting: Video call with Deira branch, 11:10 am.

lines.text: Here's one from my team. A customer has a company in the DIFC. Do we follow DIFC rules for him?
Lumara is an onshore bank licensed by the CBUAE, so we follow the federal law, the executive regulations and CBUAE guidance for everything we do.
The DIFC and ADGM have their own regulators and rulebooks for firms licensed there. That's their regime, not ours.
So a DIFC company is simply a customer to us, risk-assessed like any other?
Exactly. And the predicate offence doesn't have to be proven first. If the facts point to crime, we escalate.
Then my tellers need to stop waiting for proof before they speak up.

cards.title: Onshore banks vs the financial free zones
cards.caption: A customer based in a free zone does not change which rules an onshore bank must follow.

cards.title: Real case: the 2025 reset of UAE AML law
cards.body:
In 2025 the UAE rebuilt its AML framework in two steps.

- **Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025** was issued on 30 September 2025 and entered into force two weeks after publication, replacing Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018. It made proliferation financing an offence in its own right and raised penalties.
- **Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025** was issued on 29 October 2025 as the new executive regulations, entering into force 30 days after publication and repealing Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019.

The law kept earlier regulations and circulars alive only where they do not conflict with it, until replacements are issued.

**Lesson for Lumara:** procedures and older guidance that quote 2018 or 2019 article numbers must be mapped to the new texts. A procedure that cites a repealed article can confuse staff and will be questioned in an inspection.

cards.title: How the UAE framework reached today

items.label: Decree-Law No. 20
items.detail: Earlier AML/CFT law, now repealed by the 2025 decree-law.

items.label: Cabinet Decision No. 10
items.detail: Earlier executive regulations, repealed by Resolution 134 of 2025.

items.label: Cabinet Resolution 74
items.detail: Legal basis for targeted financial sanctions; still in force.

items.label: Decree-Law No. 10 issued
items.detail: New AML/CFT/CPF law with a standalone PF offence.

items.label: Resolution 134 issued
items.detail: New executive regulations replacing the 2019 decision.

items.label: UAE presides MENAFATF
items.detail: UAE takes the presidency of the regional FATF-style body.

cards.title: Key terms of the UAE framework

cards.back: The underlying crime that generated the money. Its perpetrator need not be convicted for laundering to be proven.
The authority that supervises a sector for AML/CFT/CPF. For onshore banks, that is the CBUAE.
The independent Financial Intelligence Unit within the Central Bank. It is the only recipient of suspicious transaction reports.
The FIU's electronic reporting platform, also used for sanctions match reports to the EOCN.
A ban on moving, transferring or disposing of funds while they stay with the holder, for as long as the order lasts.
The committee chaired by the CBUAE Governor that sets national AML/CFT/CPF strategy and assesses national risk.

cards.title: The cash for a villa
cards.situation: A walk-in customer at Deira wants to deposit a large amount of cash to complete a villa purchase. He says it comes from 'a business back home' and has no documents. A teller tells Rashid: 'Nobody has proven any crime. We can't refuse money just because of a feeling.'

choices.text: Accept the deposit: without proof of a predicate crime, there is nothing to escalate
choices.outcome: This misreads the law. Knowledge can be inferred from the facts, and the bank does not need proof of a crime to report suspicion. Waiting for proof is how laundering succeeds.

choices.text: Apply the bank's CDD and source-of-funds steps and, if the story doesn't hold together, raise an internal report to the compliance officer without alerting the customer
choices.outcome: Right. The teller's job is not to prove a crime but to apply CDD and escalate suspicion. The compliance officer then decides whether to file with the FIU. The customer is not told.

choices.text: Refuse the deposit and tell the customer the bank suspects money laundering
choices.outcome: Declining may be appropriate, but telling the customer about the suspicion risks tipping off, which is an offence. The concern still needs to reach the compliance officer.

choices.text: Accept it but split it across two days so the amount looks smaller
choices.outcome: This would make the bank part of the problem. Splitting to avoid scrutiny is itself a red flag, never a workaround.

cards.title: What is at stake under the 2025 law

items.label: Prison for money laundering
items.detail: Plus a fine of AED 100,000 to 5 million, or the value of the property if greater (Article 26).

items.label: Fine for a legal person
items.detail: When its representatives commit ML, TF or PF in its name, or the property value if greater (Article 27).

items.label: Top supervisory fine
items.detail: Per violation, from a minimum of AED 10,000, imposed by the supervisor (Article 17).

items.label: FIU suspension power
items.detail: The FIU head can suspend a suspected transaction for up to ten working days (Article 5).

cards.question: A prosecutor cannot obtain a conviction for the fraud that generated some funds. Can the person who moved those funds still be convicted of money laundering?
options: No, the fraud must first be proven in a separate trial
Only if the funds exceed a legal threshold
Only if the person also took part in the fraud
Yes, laundering is an independent crime and a predicate conviction is not required
cards.explanation: Article 2 treats laundering as an independent crime and states that a conviction for the predicate offence is not needed to establish the illicit source. Knowledge can be inferred from the circumstances. There is no value threshold.

cards.title: Real case: the UAE leads MENAFATF (2026)
cards.body:
In November 2025 the EOCN announced that, at the 41st plenary of the Middle East and North Africa Financial Action Task Force in Manama, the UAE was confirmed to take the group's presidency from January 2026. The secretary-general of the UAE's National Committee was named president, and the EOCN's director was named chair of the technical committee on targeted financial sanctions and sanctions evasion for 2026-2027.

**Why it matters at branch level:** the UAE now leads regional peer review on AML/CFT/CPF. International scrutiny of how well UAE banks apply the rules is high, and supervisors expect institutions to show that controls work in practice, not just on paper.

FATF standards remain the international baseline, but your daily duties come from UAE law and CBUAE supervision.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 is the UAE AML/CFT/CPF law; Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025 is its executive regulation.
The law has three offences: money laundering, terrorist financing and the standalone proliferation financing offence.
No predicate conviction is needed, knowledge can be inferred from facts, and a bank itself can be criminally liable.
The CBUAE supervises onshore banks; the UAE FIU receives STRs via goAML; the EOCN oversees targeted financial sanctions.
The DIFC and ADGM have separate regulators and rulebooks; Lumara follows the onshore federal framework.

cards.prompt: Think of your own role. Which of the three offences could most realistically pass through the products or customers you handle, and who in your institution would you go to first if you noticed it?

quiz.question: Which instrument is the current federal AML/CFT/CPF law for UAE onshore banks?
options: Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018
Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019
Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025
Cabinet Resolution No. 74 of 2020
quiz.explanation: Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 repealed Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018. Cabinet Decision 10 of 2019 was the old executive regulation, and Resolution 74 of 2020 is the sanctions framework, not the main AML law.

quiz.question: What is Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025?
options: The decree-law's executive regulations
The UAE Local Terrorist List issued by the Cabinet
The CBUAE's corporate governance standards for banks
A CBUAE circular on consumer protection
quiz.explanation: Resolution 134 of 2025 sets the executive regulations under Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025, replacing Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019. It holds the detailed rules on risk, CDD, reporting, training and records.

quiz.question: Which body is the exclusive recipient of suspicious transaction reports from UAE banks?
options: The CBUAE banking supervision department
The UAE Financial Intelligence Unit
The Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation
The Public Prosecution
quiz.explanation: Article 11 of the decree-law establishes the FIU within the Central Bank, acting independently, and makes it the exclusive recipient of STRs. The EOCN handles sanctions and the CBUAE supervises.

quiz.question: Who chairs the UAE National Committee for combating money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing?
options: The Minister of Interior
The head of the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit
The Director of the EOCN
The Governor of the Central Bank
quiz.explanation: Article 13 of the decree-law establishes the National Committee under the chairmanship of the Governor of the Central Bank. Its secretary-general acts as deputy chair.

quiz.question: A Lumara customer company is licensed in the ADGM and banks with Lumara onshore. Which AML regime governs Lumara's handling of the account?
options: The FSRA's ADGM rulebook, because the customer is licensed there
A choice between the two regimes made by the customer
The federal law, its executive regulations and CBUAE supervision
No AML regime, because free-zone firms are exempt
quiz.explanation: Lumara is an onshore bank licensed by the CBUAE, so its own obligations come from the federal framework and CBUAE supervision. The ADGM's FSRA regulates firms licensed in ADGM; that does not change Lumara's regime.

quiz.question: Which statement about terrorist financing under Article 3 of the 2025 decree-law is correct?
options: Only funds that are proceeds of a crime can amount to terrorist financing
The funds must actually be used in a terrorist act
Virtual assets fall outside the offence
Lawfully earned funds can still be terrorist financing
quiz.explanation: Article 3 covers funds from legitimate or illegitimate sources, regardless of whether they were actually used in an attack, and expressly includes digital systems and virtual assets.

quiz.question: A teller says she cannot escalate a deposit because nobody has proven the customer committed a crime. Under the 2025 law, which point best corrects her?
options: Escalation is needed only once the police have opened a criminal case
Tellers may escalate only amounts above AED 55,000
Only the compliance officer may form a suspicion
Knowledge can be inferred and no predicate conviction is needed
quiz.explanation: Article 2 makes laundering an independent crime, says a predicate conviction is not required and allows knowledge to be inferred from objective circumstances. Staff escalate on suspicion, not proof.

quiz.question: What changed for proliferation financing under Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025?
options: It was moved entirely into Cabinet Resolution 74 of 2020
It became an administrative breach only
It became a standalone criminal offence in the law
It was limited to trade finance transactions
quiz.explanation: Article 3(3) of the 2025 decree-law sets out proliferation financing as a crime in its own right, with penalties in Article 26. TFS implementation still relies on Resolution 74 of 2020.

quiz.question: The FIU suspects a transaction at Lumara is linked to a crime and wants it held while it analyses STRs. What can the head of the FIU order under Article 5?
options: Suspension for up to ten working days
Permanent confiscation of the funds by the FIU
Suspension of the transaction for up to ninety working days
Revocation of the customer's residency
quiz.explanation: Article 5(1) lets the head of the FIU suspend a suspected transaction without prior notice for up to ten working days. Freezing of funds can last up to thirty days, extendable by the Attorney General; confiscation is for courts.

quiz.question: Senior managers ask whether Lumara itself, not just an employee, can be criminally liable for laundering. What does the decree-law say?
options: No, only individuals can commit the offences under the decree-law
Only if the board formally approved each of the transactions involved
Only for terrorist financing, not money laundering
Yes, if the crime is committed intentionally in its name or for its account
quiz.explanation: Article 4 makes a legal person criminally liable when any of the crimes is intentionally committed in its name or for its account, without affecting the personal liability of the individual. Article 27 sets its fines.

sessions.title: Risk-Based Approach, CDD, Beneficial Owners and PEPs
sessions.summary: Apply Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025 at onboarding: assess risk, know when CDD is triggered, identify beneficial owners, handle PEPs, decide between enhanced and simplified measures and know when to walk away.
objectives: Apply the risk factors and documentation duties of the 2025 executive regulations
Identify when CDD must be applied, including the occasional transaction and wire transfer thresholds
Work through the beneficial ownership cascade for companies and trusts
Apply the PEP rules for foreign, domestic and international organisation PEPs
Decide when to apply enhanced measures, simplified measures or to decline the relationship

cards.title: A company with layers
cards.setting: Corporate onboarding desk, Lumara Bank, Dubai. 10:00 am.

lines.text: Big one for us: Orion Bay General Trading wants an operating account and trade lines. The paperwork looks complete.
The shareholder list shows two companies, one registered abroad. I can't see a single human name yet.
Then the file isn't complete. Under the 2025 regulations we must identify the natural persons behind it and understand the control structure.
The relationship manager says one owner's father is a minister in another country. Does that kill the deal?
Not automatically. It changes what we must do and who must approve it.
Welcome to the Onboarding Gate. Let's work out who is really there and how much risk we're taking.

scenes.heading: Identify the risks
scenes.narration: Article 5 requires each bank to identify and assess its money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing risks, in proportion to its size and business.

scenes.heading: Use every lens
scenes.narration: Consider customer risk, country and geographic risk, and product, service, transaction and delivery channel risk, and take the National Risk Assessment into account.

scenes.heading: Write it down
scenes.narration: Document how you assessed the risks, keep the study up to date and provide it to the authorities on request.

scenes.heading: Match the controls
scenes.narration: Apply enhanced due diligence where risk is high. Simplified measures are allowed only for identified low risk, in coordination with the supervisor, and never when crime is suspected.

cards.title: The risk cycle every bank runs

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Customers, countries, products, services, transactions and channels.

items.label: Assess
items.detail: Rate likelihood and impact, using the National Risk Assessment.

items.label: Document
items.detail: Record method and results; give them to the supervisor on request.

items.label: Mitigate
items.detail: Policies approved by senior management; EDD for high risk.

items.label: Monitor and update
items.detail: Review as products, customers and threats change.

cards.question: Lumara's retail team proposes simplified due diligence for a low-risk payroll account product. Which condition makes simplified measures unavailable for a particular customer?
options: The customer is a UAE resident
There is a suspicion that a crime is being committed
The account is opened at a branch rather than online
The customer's salary is paid by a government entity
cards.explanation: Article 5(3) allows simplified measures only where low risk is identified, in coordination with the supervisor, and never where there is suspicion of a crime. Residency, channel or employer do not on their own rule simplified measures in or out.

cards.title: When CDD is triggered (Article 7)
cards.caption: Thresholds are from Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025. Your bank's policy may set stricter internal limits.

items.label: New business relationship
items.detail: Before or during account opening or the start of the relationship.

items.label: Suspicion of a crime
items.detail: Whatever the amount and whatever the customer's history.

items.label: Doubts about existing data
items.detail: When earlier identification data seems inaccurate or inadequate.

items.label: Occasional transactions
items.detail: AED 55,000 or more, as one transaction or several that appear linked.

items.label: Occasional wire transfers
items.detail: AED 3,500 or more for a customer without a business relationship.

cards.title: Enhanced, standard or simplified?
cards.prompt: Sort each measure into the level of due diligence it belongs to under Article 5.

items.text: Obtaining senior management approval to start or continue the relationship
Taking reasonable measures to establish source of funds and source of wealth
Requiring the first payment through an account in the customer's name at a bank with equivalent standards
Identifying the customer and verifying identity from a reliable, independent source
Understanding the purpose and intended nature of the relationship
Updating customer data at longer intervals
Verifying identity after the relationship starts
Reducing the frequency of transaction monitoring

cards.title: Finding the human behind the company
cards.body:
Article 10 of Resolution 134 sets a **cascade** for legal persons. Take reasonable measures to verify each step from reliable, independent sources:

1. **Ownership:** the natural person who ultimately owns **25% or more**, alone or jointly with others.
2. **Control by other means:** if ownership leaves doubt, or nobody controls through ownership, the person exercising legal or actual control in any other way.
3. **Senior management:** if no one is found, the natural person or persons holding a senior management position.

For **trusts and similar arrangements**, identify the settlor, trustee, protector, beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and anyone else with ultimate effective control.

A company listed on a securities market with adequate disclosure rules, or its majority-owned subsidiary, may be exempt from shareholder identification (Article 11). Giving a bank false beneficial owner information is itself an offence under the decree-law.

cards.title: Walk the beneficial ownership cascade
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the order Lumara applies them to a corporate customer.
steps: Obtain the company's basic information: name, legal form, constitution, registered address and senior managers
Map the ownership chain through every intermediate company to natural persons
Identify any natural person owning 25% or more, alone or jointly
If ownership is unclear or nobody qualifies, identify who controls the company by other means
If still nobody is identified, record the senior managing official as beneficial owner
Verify the identities from reliable, independent sources and record the result

lines.text: Found him. Orion Bay is 40% owned by a holding company that belongs entirely to the son of a serving deputy minister abroad.
The son isn't a politician. He runs a logistics business.
The regulations treat immediate family of a PEP, such as children, as part of the PEP definition. And he's the beneficial owner.
So we refuse him?
No blanket refusal. For a foreign PEP we need senior management approval, reasonable measures on source of funds and wealth, and enhanced ongoing monitoring.
Then let's build the file properly and let the right people decide.

cards.back: Someone who holds or held a prominent public function in another country, such as a head of state, senior politician, senior judge or military officer.
Someone who holds or held a prominent public function in the UAE.
Someone who manages or held a prominent function in an international organisation, such as a director or board member.
Immediate family of a PEP, such as spouses, children and their spouses, and parents.
People with joint beneficial ownership or close business or social ties with a PEP, or sole owners of a vehicle set up for a PEP's benefit.
The definition covers people who were previously entrusted with prominent functions, so stepping down does not end the assessment.

items.label: Senior management approval
items.right: When the relationship is high risk

items.label: Source of funds and wealth
items.right: When the relationship is high risk

cards.title: Orion Bay: what do you recommend?
cards.situation: Orion Bay General Trading's 40% beneficial owner is the son of a serving foreign deputy minister. The documents explain a logistics business with expected monthly flows of about AED 4 million. The relationship manager wants to open the account today because a competitor bank is also courting the client.

choices.text: Decline the client outright because PEP-linked customers are too risky
choices.outcome: Blanket refusal is not what the rules require and can push risk elsewhere without managing it. The regulations expect you to assess and control PEP risk, not avoid every PEP.

choices.text: Open today with standard CDD and review the PEP link at the first periodic review
choices.outcome: This skips mandatory steps. For a foreign PEP, senior management approval, source of funds and wealth measures and enhanced monitoring are needed before the relationship starts.

choices.text: Treat the owner as a foreign PEP: verify the structure, establish source of funds and wealth, obtain senior management approval and set enhanced monitoring before opening
choices.outcome: Correct. Family members of PEPs fall within the definition, and for foreign PEPs Article 16 requires these steps before establishing the relationship. Commercial pressure does not change the sequence.

choices.text: Ask the client to move the son's shares into a nominee's name so the PEP link disappears from the file
choices.outcome: This would help disguise beneficial ownership. Knowingly assisting concealment is exactly what the law targets.

cards.question: Lumara cannot verify who ultimately controls a prospective corporate customer, despite repeated requests. What does Article 14 require?
options: Open the account with a note to complete the file within a year
Open the account but block outgoing transfers above AED 55,000
Do not open the relationship or execute the transaction, and consider an STR
Ask the customer to sign a declaration and proceed
cards.explanation: Article 14(1) prohibits establishing or continuing a relationship, or executing a transaction, when CDD cannot be applied, and asks the bank to consider an STR. A declaration or a temporary restriction does not cure missing CDD.

cards.title: When CDD itself could tip off
cards.body:
Article 14(2) covers a delicate moment: you suspect a crime, and asking more CDD questions would alert the customer.

- You **may stop** the CDD process in that case.
- You **must file** a suspicious transaction report with the FIU, explaining why CDD was not completed.
- Never open or keep **anonymous or obviously fictitious accounts**, and never deal with **shell banks** (Article 15).

Common mistake: carrying on with a long questionnaire that makes the customer realise you are suspicious.

cards.title: Correspondent banking under Article 26
cards.prompt: Match each requirement to what it means before Lumara opens a correspondent relationship.

pairs.right: Never enter or continue a relationship with a shell bank or anyone who lets shell banks use its accounts
Understand its business, reputation and supervision, including past AML investigations or actions
Assess the respondent's own anti-crime controls
Obtain senior management approval before establishing a new relationship
Confirm the respondent has done CDD on customers with direct access and can share it on request

cards.title: Customer risk at a glance
cards.caption: A simplified view. Article 5 asks you to weigh all the factors together before deciding the level of measures.

items.label: Watch the product
items.detail: Lower-risk customer using a higher-risk product, such as trade lines: monitor product use closely.

items.label: Full EDD
items.detail: Higher-risk customer and product, such as a PEP-linked trader: EDD and senior approval.

items.label: Standard or simplified
items.detail: Lower-risk customer and product, where policy and the supervisor allow it.

items.label: Customer-focused EDD
items.detail: Higher-risk customer, simple product: verify ownership and source of wealth.

cards.title: Worked example: relying on another bank's CDD
cards.body:
Lumara is asked to rely on a regulated bank in the same financial group that already onboarded a customer. Article 20 allows reliance on a third party for identification, beneficial ownership and understanding the business, but:

- Lumara **remains responsible** for the accuracy of the measures.
- The third party must be **regulated and supervised** and meet UAE-standard CDD and record keeping.
- Lumara must **immediately obtain** the identification data and be able to get document copies without delay.
- Country risk must be considered, including countries the National Committee identifies as high risk.

Outsourcing CDD work to an agent that follows Lumara's own procedures under Lumara's control is not 'reliance' in this sense: it is Lumara's own CDD.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Assess customer, country, product, service, transaction and channel risk, document it and use the National Risk Assessment.
CDD applies to new relationships, suspicion, doubtful data, occasional transactions of AED 55,000+ and occasional wires of AED 3,500+.
Beneficial ownership cascade: 25%+ ownership, then control by other means, then senior management.
Foreign PEPs always need senior approval, source of funds and wealth measures and enhanced monitoring; domestic PEPs when high risk.
If CDD cannot be completed, do not proceed and consider an STR; if CDD would tip off, stop and report.

cards.prompt: Recall a customer file you worked on or reviewed. Could you name every natural person who owned or controlled it, and would the file convince a CBUAE inspector? What would you add?

quiz.question: Which risk factors does Article 5 of Resolution 134 require a bank to consider before deciding its overall risk level?
options: Only the customer's nationality, income and length of residence in the UAE
Only the risks named by the customer's employer
Customer, country, product, service, transaction and channel risks
Only products launched in the last year
quiz.explanation: Article 5(1)(a) requires all relevant factors, including customer, country and geographic, product, service, transaction and delivery channel risks, taking into account the National Risk Assessment.

quiz.question: A walk-in customer with no account wants to send an occasional wire transfer of AED 4,000 abroad. Does Resolution 134 require CDD?
options: No, CDD for occasional transactions only starts at AED 55,000 or more
Yes, the AED 3,500 wire transfer threshold applies
No, CDD is only for account holders
Only if the beneficiary country is high risk
quiz.explanation: Article 7(2)(b) requires CDD for occasional wire transfers of AED 3,500 or more. The AED 55,000 threshold applies to other occasional transactions.

quiz.question: A non-customer makes three cash purchases of cashier's cheques on the same day, AED 20,000 each, for the same beneficiary. What applies?
options: CDD, because the linked transactions total AED 55,000 or more
Nothing, because each individual transaction stays below AED 55,000 on its own
CDD only if the customer asks for a receipt
A sanctions report to the EOCN
quiz.explanation: Article 7(2)(a) requires CDD for occasional transactions of AED 55,000 or more, whether a single transaction or several that appear linked. Together these total AED 60,000.

quiz.question: Under Article 10, what is the first test for identifying the beneficial owner of a company?
options: Any shareholder owning 10% or more, directly or through a holding company
A natural person owning 25% or more, alone or jointly
The company's registered agent
The person who signs the account opening form
quiz.explanation: Article 10(1)(a) starts with the natural person who ultimately owns a controlling interest of 25% or more, alone or jointly. Control by other means and senior management follow if needed.

quiz.question: A company has five shareholders with 20% each and no one controls it in any other way. Who should Lumara record as beneficial owner?
options: Nobody: the company has no beneficial owner
The largest corporate shareholder
All five shareholders as joint beneficial owners by default
The natural person or persons holding senior management positions
quiz.explanation: No one meets the 25% test and no one controls by other means, so Article 10(1)(c) requires identifying the senior management official or officials.

quiz.question: Which group is included in the definition of a politically exposed person in Resolution 134?
options: Any customer who works in a federal or local government entity in any role
Only serving heads of state
Immediate family such as spouses, children and parents
Only people living in the UAE
quiz.explanation: The definition covers people with prominent public functions in the UAE or abroad, including former holders, plus immediate family and known close associates.

quiz.question: For a domestic PEP whose relationship is not assessed as high risk, which measure is required?
options: Senior management approval in every case, whatever the risk rating
Refusal of the relationship
Monthly source-of-wealth recertification by the customer
Adequate measures to find out whether the customer is a PEP
quiz.explanation: Article 16(1)(b) requires adequate measures to identify domestic and international organisation PEPs, and applies approval, source of funds and wealth checks and enhanced monitoring when the relationship is high risk.

quiz.question: A relationship manager is under pressure to open a foreign PEP's account today and complete approvals next week. What does Article 16 require?
options: Senior management approval before the relationship starts
Approval within one month of opening, provided enhanced monitoring starts at once
Approval only if deposits exceed AED 55,000
No approval if the PEP is a former official
quiz.explanation: For foreign PEPs, Article 16(1)(a) requires senior management approval before establishing or continuing the relationship, plus source of funds and wealth measures and enhanced monitoring. Former PEPs remain within the definition.

quiz.question: While collecting CDD, an analyst realises further questions would reveal that the bank suspects the customer. What may the bank do?
options: Complete all CDD questions anyway and decide later
Close the account and explain the suspicion to the customer
Ask the customer to sign a statement of good conduct
Stop the CDD process and file an STR stating why CDD was not completed
quiz.explanation: Article 14(2) allows a bank that suspects a crime to refrain from CDD if it would alert the customer, provided it files an STR giving the reasons.

quiz.question: Lumara relies on another regulated bank to carry out CDD on a shared customer. Who remains responsible for the accuracy of the CDD?
options: The third-party bank becomes solely responsible
Lumara remains responsible
The CBUAE, which approved the third party
The customer, who signed the forms
quiz.explanation: Article 20 permits reliance on a regulated, supervised third party, but the relying institution remains responsible and must obtain the CDD data immediately and copies of documents without delay.

sessions.title: Suspicious Transaction Reporting, Tipping Off and Records
sessions.summary: Follow suspicion from the branch to the UAE FIU: internal escalation, the compliance officer's decision, filing through goAML without delay, the ban on tipping off, legal protection for good-faith reporters and the five-year record-keeping rule.
objectives: Explain the duty to report suspicion to the UAE FIU without delay and regardless of value
Follow Lumara's internal escalation path from employee to compliance officer to goAML
Recognise and avoid tipping off, and know who the prohibition applies to
Apply the record-keeping rules, including the five-year minimum and the latest trigger date

cards.title: The alert that wouldn't go away
cards.setting: Transaction monitoring room, Lumara head office, Abu Dhabi. 9:20 am.

lines.text: Look at this personal account. Cash deposits by different people at four branches, every one just a little under our internal review limit.
Within a day the balance goes out as transfers to three overseas accounts. The customer says he's a car dealer, but there's no business account.
What does your gut say, and what does the evidence say?
Gut says structuring. Evidence says the pattern doesn't match his profile at all.
(calling in) And he's in my branch right now, asking why yesterday's transfer is 'stuck'.
Then this is the Signal Room. We'll decide what to report, how fast, and exactly what Rashid can and cannot say to him.

scenes.heading: Someone notices
scenes.narration: A teller, analyst or relationship manager sees something that doesn't fit the customer's profile. Suspicion, not proof, is the trigger.

scenes.heading: Report inside first
scenes.narration: The employee raises an internal report to the compliance officer using the bank's channel, and does not discuss it with the customer.

scenes.heading: The compliance officer decides
scenes.narration: The compliance officer reviews the data and decides whether to notify the FIU or keep the matter on file, recording the reasons, in full confidentiality.

scenes.heading: File without delay
scenes.narration: If there is suspicion or reasonable grounds for it, the bank files a detailed report through goAML immediately, whatever the amount, and answers FIU follow-up requests promptly.

scenes.heading: The FIU can act
scenes.narration: The head of the FIU can suspend a suspected transaction for up to ten working days, or freeze funds for up to thirty days, extendable by the Attorney General.

items.label: Spot
items.detail: Unusual activity, behaviour or documents compared with what you know.

items.label: Escalate
items.detail: Internal report to the compliance officer, the same day where possible.

items.label: Review
items.detail: Compliance officer examines records, alerts and CDD data.

items.label: Decide and document
items.detail: Report to the FIU, or keep on file with written reasons.

items.label: File in goAML
items.detail: Detailed STR with all available information, without delay.

items.label: Follow up
items.detail: Answer FIU requests promptly; review the relationship.

cards.title: Escalate or not?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each observation should go to the compliance officer as an internal report.
buckets: No escalation needed on its own

items.text: A customer asks how much cash he can deposit before 'anyone asks questions'
Several unrelated people deposit cash into one personal account at different branches
A salaried customer's account suddenly receives and forwards large business-like transfers
A customer's documents show different dates of birth on two IDs
A teacher's account receives her monthly salary and pays school fees
A pensioner withdraws a similar amount of cash each month for household use
A restaurant deposits takings that match its seasonal pattern and licence
A customer abandons a transfer when asked about its purpose

cards.question: A suspicious transfer is only AED 900. What does the 2025 framework say about reporting it?
options: No report is needed below AED 3,500
Report only if similar transfers exceed AED 55,000 in a month
Report only if the customer is already high risk
Report it: the duty applies regardless of the transaction's value
cards.explanation: Both Article 18 of the decree-law and Article 18 of Resolution 134 apply the reporting duty regardless of value. The AED 3,500 and AED 55,000 figures are CDD thresholds for occasional transactions, not reporting thresholds.

cards.title: The reporting duty in the law
"Have you reported me?"
cards.setting: Deira branch, customer service desk. 11:05 am.

lines.text: (to the customer) Good morning. I understand you're asking about yesterday's transfer.
The customer leans forward and lowers his voice.
He's asking me straight out: 'Has the bank reported me to the Central Bank? Is someone investigating me?'
(on Rashid's phone, quietly) Careful. Whatever you say next could be tipping off, which is a crime for you personally, not just for the bank.
So what can I say without lying and without giving anything away?

cards.title: Rashid's answer
cards.situation: The customer insists on knowing whether he has been reported and whether 'the authorities' are looking at him. An STR is being prepared, and the FIU has not yet responded. Rashid wants to keep the customer calm without breaking the law.

choices.text: Tell him honestly that compliance has filed a report, so he understands the delay
choices.outcome: This is tipping off. Disclosing that a report has been or is about to be filed is prohibited and punishable for the individual employee.

choices.text: Say it is 'just routine checks by the FIU' and should clear soon
choices.outcome: This still reveals that the FIU is involved, which is information about a report or investigation. It is tipping off dressed up as reassurance.

choices.text: Explain that the transfer is under standard processing, that he cannot comment on individual reviews, and pass the conversation to compliance
choices.outcome: Best answer. Rashid gives a neutral, true response, discloses nothing about reports or investigations, and lets the compliance officer manage next steps.

choices.text: Release the transfer so the customer leaves happy and the issue goes away
choices.outcome: Releasing a payment to avoid an awkward conversation ignores the suspicion and could breach any FIU suspension. It does not make the duty to report go away.

items.label: Telling the customer
items.left: Saying an STR was or will be filed
items.right: Saying a transaction is being processed

items.label: Investigations
items.right: Following normal CDD and policy steps

cards.question: Who does the tipping-off prohibition in Resolution 134 apply to?
options: The bank and its directors, officers and employees
Only the compliance officer who filed the report
Only front-line staff who meet the customer
Only the bank as a legal entity
cards.explanation: Article 19 of Resolution 134 bars the institution and its directors, officers and employees from disclosing, directly or indirectly, that a report has been or will be filed or that an investigation is under way. Article 29(1) of the decree-law punishes it with prison and/or a fine of at least AED 50,000.

cards.back: Suspicious transaction report filed with the UAE FIU through goAML when there is suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect.
The employee's report to the compliance officer. It starts the process; the compliance officer decides on filing.
Telling anyone, directly or indirectly, that a report has been or will be filed, or that an investigation is under way.
Good-faith reporters are protected from criminal, civil and administrative liability for breaching confidentiality.
A serious failure of care. Failing to report through gross negligence is itself an offence, not only deliberate silence.
Categories selected in goAML to describe why a report is filed, including sanctions-evasion reasons.

cards.title: Records that survive scrutiny
cards.body:
Article 25 of Resolution 134 sets record keeping:

- Keep **transaction records** for **at least five years** from completion of the transaction or end of the relationship.
- Keep **CDD records**, account files, correspondence, ID copies, **STRs and analysis**, and **CCTV and ATM recordings** for at least five years.
- Count from the **latest** relevant date: end of relationship, account closure, completion of an occasional transaction, end of a supervisory inspection, end of an investigation or a final court judgment.
- Organise records so **individual transactions can be reconstructed** and provided promptly on request.

cards.title: Which five years? A retention example
cards.caption: Article 25 counts the period from the most recent of the listed events.

items.label: Account opened
items.detail: CDD file created for the customer.

items.label: STR filed
items.detail: Report and analysis join the CDD records.

items.label: Account closed
items.detail: One possible start of the five-year clock.

items.label: Investigation ends
items.detail: A later trigger, so the clock restarts here.

items.label: Earliest disposal
items.detail: Five years after the latest trigger, not 2031.

cards.title: Why each record matters
cards.prompt: Match each record to the reason it must be kept and retrievable.

pairs.right: Let the bank reconstruct individual transactions as evidence
Show what the bank knew, why it reported and when
Prove who the customer and beneficial owners were
Trace originator and beneficiary across borders
Show why a sanctions alert needed no report

cards.title: Inside a good STR
cards.prompt: Arrange the steps the compliance team follows to prepare a goAML filing.
steps: Collect the alert, internal report and full CDD file
Review account history and linked parties to understand the pattern
Decide that grounds for suspicion exist and record the reasoning
Write a clear narrative: who, what, when, where, why it is suspicious
Attach supporting data and submit through goAML without delay
Respond promptly to any FIU request and review the relationship

cards.question: A customer's account closed in 2026, but an investigation involving the account ended in 2028. Under Article 25, from when do the five years run for the CDD records?
options: From 2026, when the account closed
From 2028, the most recent of the listed events
From the date the account was opened
From the date the STR was filed
cards.explanation: Article 25(2) counts the retention period from the most recent of several events, including account closure and completion of an investigation. Here that is 2028, so records must be kept at least until 2033.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Report suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect to the UAE FIU through goAML without delay, regardless of value, including attempts.
Staff escalate internally; the compliance officer decides whether to file and records the reasons.
Failing to report deliberately or through gross negligence is a crime; good-faith reporters are protected.
Tipping off is banned for the bank and every director, officer and employee; give neutral answers and involve compliance.
Keep records at least five years from the latest trigger, organised so transactions can be reconstructed.

cards.prompt: Imagine a customer asks you, 'Have I been reported?' Write the exact sentence you would say, then check it: does it confirm or deny anything about a report or an investigation?

quiz.question: What standard triggers the duty to file an STR under Article 18 of the decree-law?
options: Proof beyond reasonable doubt that a crime occurred, confirmed by the compliance officer
Suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect a link to the crime
A court order requesting information
A transaction of at least AED 55,000
quiz.explanation: Article 18 requires notifying the FIU when the institution suspects or has reasonable grounds to suspect that a transaction or funds are proceeds of, related to or intended for the crime, regardless of value.

quiz.question: How must Lumara submit an STR to the UAE FIU?
options: Directly through goAML, without delay
By letter to the CBUAE governor's office, copied to the supervisor
Through the EOCN Notification Alert System
By telephone to the local police
quiz.explanation: The law requires a detailed report to the FIU, directly and without delay, through the electronic system designated by the Unit, which is goAML.

quiz.question: Who decides at Lumara whether an internal report becomes an STR to the FIU?
options: The compliance officer, who records the reasons
The branch manager of the employee who raised the internal report
The relationship manager who knows the customer best
The board risk committee at its next meeting
quiz.explanation: Article 22(2) of Resolution 134 gives the compliance officer the duty to receive, examine and assess suspicious transaction data and decide whether to notify the FIU or keep the matter, stating the reasons, in confidence.

quiz.question: A transaction monitoring analyst ignores a clear alert for months because the queue was long. Which offence could apply?
options: Tipping off under Article 29 of the decree-law, because the customer was not told
Providing false beneficial owner information
Failing to report through gross negligence
Breaching a TFS instruction under Article 33
quiz.explanation: Article 28 punishes anyone who deliberately or through gross negligence violates the reporting duty in Article 18, with prison and/or a fine of AED 100,000 to 1 million.

quiz.question: A customer asks a call-centre agent why his account is under review. Which reply avoids tipping off?
options: The FIU is looking at your account, but I'm sure it will be fine in the end
Reviews follow standard procedures and I can't discuss individual cases
Compliance filed a report, so please be patient
Someone flagged your transfers as suspicious
quiz.explanation: The neutral reply discloses nothing about reports or investigations. The other answers reveal that a report exists or that authorities are involved, which Article 19 of Resolution 134 prohibits.

quiz.question: What is the minimum fine for tipping off under Article 29(1) of the 2025 decree-law, if a fine is imposed?
quiz.explanation: Article 29(1) punishes disclosure about suspicious transactions under review or about investigations with imprisonment and a fine of not less than AED 50,000, or either penalty.

quiz.question: An employee reports a suspicion in good faith, but the FIU later finds no crime. What protection applies?
options: They are protected from criminal, civil and administrative liability
The employee may be sued personally for breach of banking confidentiality by the customer
The bank must compensate the customer for any delay
The employee must repay the costs of the FIU review
quiz.explanation: Article 37 removes liability for furnishing required information or breaching confidentiality restrictions, even without full awareness of the crime, unless the report was made in bad faith to harm others.

quiz.question: For how long must Lumara keep transaction records under Resolution 134?
options: At least two years from the transaction date, or longer if the customer agrees in writing
Until the customer requests deletion
At least ten years in every case
At least five years from completion or end of the relationship
quiz.explanation: Article 25(1) requires transaction records to be kept for not less than five years from the completion of the transaction or the end of the business relationship, and made available promptly on request.

quiz.question: Which of these must be kept under Article 25 alongside CDD records?
options: CCTV and related ATM recordings
Staff lunch rosters
Marketing brochures sent to the customer
Draft emails never sent to anyone
quiz.explanation: Article 25(2) lists CDD records, monitoring results, account files, correspondence, ID copies, STRs, analysis results, CCTV and related ATM recordings and other recordings.

quiz.question: A relationship ended in 2025, a CBUAE inspection covering it finished in 2027 and a court judgment became final in 2029. When can CDD records be disposed of at the earliest?
quiz.explanation: Article 25(2) counts at least five years from the most recent listed event. The latest is the final judgment in 2029, so records must be kept until at least 2034.

sessions.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions and Counter-Proliferation
sessions.summary: Apply UAE targeted financial sanctions under Cabinet Resolution 74 of 2020 and EOCN guidance: register, screen, freeze within 24 hours, report confirmed and partial matches through goAML, apply ownership rules, and spot proliferation financing and sanctions evasion in trade.
objectives: Describe the UAE's two sanctions lists and the four TFS steps: register, screen, freeze, report
Handle confirmed matches, partial matches, false positives and negative results correctly
Apply the majority-ownership and acting-on-behalf rules for freezing
Recognise proliferation financing and sanctions-evasion red flags in trade finance
Distinguish CNMR and PNMR filings from STRs to the FIU

cards.title: 7:40 am: the alert email
cards.setting: Screening team, Lumara head office, Abu Dhabi. Early morning.

lines.text: An email from the EOCN Notification Alert System arrives: new names have been added to the UAE Local Terrorist List.
Screening rerun started. One partial hit on an existing customer: same name and date of birth, different nationality.
Then the clock is running. A confirmed match must be frozen without delay, which the EOCN defines as within 24 hours.
(joining) And while you're here: a trade client wants a letter of credit for 'industrial machine parts' routed through a third country. Something feels off.
Two different problems, two different routes. Welcome to the Freeze Vault.

cards.title: UAE targeted financial sanctions in brief

scenes.heading: Two lists
scenes.narration: UAE TFS applies to people and entities on the UAE Local Terrorist List, issued by the Cabinet, and the UN Security Council Consolidated List.

scenes.heading: The legal basis
scenes.narration: Cabinet Resolution 74 of 2020 sets the duties, and the 2025 decree-law requires banks to implement EOCN instructions on TFS at once.

scenes.heading: Register
scenes.narration: Banks register with the EOCN Notification Alert System so they receive list updates automatically.

scenes.heading: Screen
scenes.narration: Screen immediately on every list update, before onboarding, at periodic reviews or ownership changes, and before processing transactions.

scenes.heading: Freeze and prohibit
scenes.narration: On a confirmed match, freeze without delay and without prior notice, and make no funds or services available to the designated person.

scenes.heading: Report
scenes.narration: File a Confirmed Name Match Report or Partial Name Match Report through goAML within five business days of acting.

items.label: Register
items.detail: Subscribe to the EOCN Notification Alert System for list updates.

items.label: Screen
items.detail: Customers, prospects, past customers, parties, owners and signatories.

items.label: Freeze or suspend
items.detail: Freeze confirmed matches within 24 hours; suspend partial matches.

items.label: Report
items.detail: CNMR or PNMR via goAML to the EOCN and supervisor within 5 business days.

cards.title: Four screening results and what to do

items.label: Confirmed match
items.left: All key identifiers match a listed person
items.right: Freeze or reject; file a CNMR

items.label: Partial match
items.left: Some identifiers match; you cannot conclude
items.right: Suspend or reject; file a PNMR

items.label: False positive
items.left: Identifiers show it is someone else

items.label: Negative
items.right: No action beyond normal screening records

cards.question: Lumara freezes an existing customer's accounts after a confirmed match with the UAE Local Terrorist List. What reporting step follows?
options: File an STR with the FIU within thirty days
Email the customer's relationship manager and wait for EOCN contact
File a CNMR through goAML within five business days of freezing
Report at the next quarterly compliance committee
cards.explanation: EOCN guidance requires a Confirmed Name Match Report through goAML to the EOCN and the supervisor within five business days of taking the freezing measure. The freeze itself must happen without delay, within 24 hours.

cards.title: Freeze or handle differently?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation under UAE TFS rules.

items.text: Company A is 51% owned by a person on the UAE Local Terrorist List
An agent is acting on the direction of a UN-listed entity
Profits due to a designated person from a company where he holds 30%
Company B is 30% owned by a designated person, with no other link
A customer matches a name only on a foreign unilateral sanctions list
A customer is mentioned in a UN Panel of Experts report but is not listed
Interest due on an already frozen account

cards.title: Partial matches, prospects and weekends
cards.body:
EOCN guidance sets out the hard cases:

- **Partial match, existing customer:** you already hold their ID but cannot decide. **Suspend** transactions and services without delay, file a **PNMR** within five business days, and keep the suspension until the EOCN tells you through goAML whether to lift it or freeze.
- **Partial match, prospect or counterparty:** try to obtain ID documents. If you cannot within a reasonable time, which the guidance puts at **10 business days**, reject the transaction and file a PNMR.
- **False positive:** no report, but **document** why.
- **Weekends and holidays:** have procedures so listed funds cannot be accessed; if nothing operates, screening starts from the first minute of business.

Freezes have **no time limit**: they last until delisting or an EOCN cancellation. Do not tell the customer a freeze is coming.

cards.title: Joseph's letter of credit
cards.setting: Trade finance desk, Lumara Bank, Dubai. 2:15 pm.

lines.text: The client, a general trading company, wants an LC for precision machine parts. The goods description is vague and the end user is a firm in a third country.
Their trade licence is for building materials. And the payment is coming from a company that isn't on the contract.
None of the names are on the lists. So sanctions-wise we're clear, aren't we?
Not so fast. No list match means no CNMR, but proliferation financing rarely uses listed names. These are classic red flags.
Some machine parts are dual-use goods on the UAE Control List, and the EOCN licenses their export. We need to ask the right questions.

cards.back: Funding weapons of mass destruction, their delivery systems or related materials, including dual-use goods. A standalone offence since 2025.
Items with civil and military uses. The UAE Control List under Cabinet Resolution 50 of 2020 sets which are controlled.
The EOCN reviews permits for import, export, re-export and transit of controlled items, looking at specifications, end use and end user.
Using fronts, false documents, odd routes or third-party payers to get round sanctions without any listed name appearing.
EOCN guidance identifies North Korea and Iran as states subject to UN TFS linked to proliferation.
EOCN expects all staff to know PF basics, with extra training for compliance, audit and trade finance.

cards.title: What should Joseph do with the LC?
cards.situation: The LC is for loosely described precision machine parts, the applicant's licence covers building materials, the end user sits in a third country, the route is circuitous, and a company not named in the contract will pay. No party matches the UAE or UN lists.

choices.text: Issue the LC: no listed names means no sanctions problem
choices.outcome: Screening is only one control. Proliferation financing typically avoids listed names, and these red flags call for enhanced checks, not approval.

choices.text: Pause, request a precise goods description, end-user details and any export permit, escalate to compliance, and support an STR if the explanations do not hold
choices.outcome: Best answer. This applies EOCN red flags and the bank's enhanced measures, keeps the decision with compliance, and uses the STR route for suspected sanctions evasion.

choices.text: File a CNMR so the EOCN can decide
choices.outcome: CNMRs and PNMRs are only for matches against the UAE Local Terrorist List or the UN list. Suspected evasion without a match goes to the FIU as an STR.

choices.text: Tell the client the bank suspects a weapons link and ask them to explain
choices.outcome: This risks tipping off. Ask for normal trade information without revealing the suspicion.

items.label: All trade transactions
items.detail: Documentary checks and screening on every party, vessel and owner.

items.label: Goods that may be dual-use
items.detail: Check against the UAE Control List and ask about permits.

items.label: Odd route, payer or end user
items.detail: Third-party payers, transhipment hubs, licence mismatch.

items.label: Escalate to compliance
items.detail: Enhanced review with the trade and compliance teams.

items.label: STR to the FIU via goAML
items.detail: When suspicion of PF or evasion remains.

cards.title: Which report fits?
cards.prompt: Match each situation to the right goAML route or action.

pairs.left: Confirmed match on the UAE Local Terrorist List
pairs.right: Freeze without delay and file a CNMR
Suspend or reject and file a PNMR

pairs.left: Suspected evasion with no list match
pairs.right: File an STR with the FIU

pairs.left: Match only on a foreign unilateral list
pairs.right: Consult the CBUAE and consider an STR

pairs.left: Alert disproved by date of birth and ID
pairs.right: Record the false positive internally
